modules.title: The Unified Mathematical Spine
modules.summary: College algebra through probability and statistics in the verified course order: equations and functions, trigonometry and the unit circle, precalculus (complex numbers, vectors, limits preview), calculus I (limits, derivatives, integrals, the Fundamental Theorem), calculus II (techniques, series, Taylor), discrete mathematics (logic, proofs, combinatorics, graphs), linear algebra (eigenvalues, least squares, SVD, matrix calculus for ML), probability and statistics (distributions, Bayes/MLE/MAP, LLN/CLT, regression, hypothesis testing).
objectives: Solve equations and work functions fluently: composition, inverses, graphs.
Differentiate and integrate: rules, applications, the Fundamental Theorem.
Prove: induction, contradiction, invariants — discrete math as a writing discipline.
Diagonalize: eigenvalues, SVD, least squares — linear algebra for ML.
Reason under uncertainty: Bayes, MLE, CLT, regression, testing.

notes.title: Algebra to calculus: the climb
notes.body:
**College algebra**: equations/inequalities, **functions and graphs** (the core object — domain, range, composition, inverses), polynomials/rationals, **exponentials and logarithms** (inverse pair — the growth/decay language).

**Trigonometry**: right-triangle ratios, the **unit circle** (every identity lives here), graphs, identities/equations.

**Precalculus**: composite/inverse functions, **complex numbers** (a+bi — the algebraic closure), vectors/matrices, conics, series, the **limits preview**.

**Calculus I**: **limits and continuity** (the epsilon-delta idea), **derivatives** (definition → rules → chain rule), applications (optimization, related rates), **integrals and the Fundamental Theorem** (differentiation and integration are inverses).

**Calculus II**: integration techniques (substitution, parts, partial fractions), applications (volumes, arc length), parametric/polar/vector functions, **series and Taylor expansions** (convergence tests; Taylor = local polynomial approximation).

- The chain rule is the whole game in disguise — backprop is the chain rule at scale
- Taylor series: approximate locally, bound the error (Lagrange remainder)
- Fluency gate: differentiate/integrate the standard forms without pausing

notes.title: Discrete mathematics: the CS dialect
notes.body:
**Logic and proofs**: propositional/predicate logic, **proof techniques** (direct, contradiction, contrapositive, induction). **Sets, functions, combinatorics** (counting: product/sum rules, pigeonhole, binomial).

**Graphs**: the universal model — paths, cycles, trees, coloring, Euler/Hamilton. **Cryptography and automata previews**: modular arithmetic → RSA; finite automata → the computation model.

- Combinatorics is organized counting — every 'how many' reduces to product/sum/choose
- Graph modeling: when stuck, draw the graph — half of algorithms is seeing the graph
- This module gates IL-03's algorithms and IL-08's theory — no induction, no algorithms

notes.title: Linear algebra and probability
notes.body:
**Linear algebra**: vectors/matrices, **eigenvalues/eigenvectors** (the directions that don't rotate), **least squares** (projection — the geometry of regression), **SVD** (the everything-decomposition: PCA, compression, latent factors), **matrix calculus for ML** (gradients of vector functions).

**Probability and statistics**: random variables and **distributions** (the zoo: normal, binomial, Poisson, exponential), **Bayes** (update beliefs), **MLE/MAP** (fit by likelihood), **LLN and CLT** (averages converge; sums go normal), **regression and hypothesis testing** (p-values, confidence — and their misuses).

- Eigenvectors: where the matrix acts by scaling — PCA, PageRank, quantum states
- Bayes: P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) — the update rule for all reasoning under uncertainty
- CLT: the reason normal distributions are everywhere — sums of small effects
- SVD: A = UΣVᵀ — rank, compression, and latent structure in one factorization

cards.back: ln b / ln a — change of base. Exponentials and logs are inverses.
(f∘g)' = f'(g(x))·g'(x). Backprop is the chain rule at scale.
Differentiation and integration are inverses: ∫ₐᵇ f' = f(b)−f(a).
Local polynomial approximation: f(x) ≈ Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!. Bound error with Lagrange remainder.
Base → hypothesis → step. The domino principle.
n+1 items in n boxes → some box has 2+. Deceptively powerful.
Av = λv — the direction the matrix only scales.
A = UΣVᵀ — rank, compression, latent factors in one factorization.
P(H|E) = P(E|H)P(H)/P(E) — update beliefs with evidence.
Sums of many small independent effects → normal. Why normals are everywhere.

quiz.explain: Integration by parts: u=x, dv=eˣdx → xeˣ − eˣ = (x−1)eˣ.
Diagonal matrix — eigenvalues on the diagonal.
Bayes: base rate dominates — (0.99×0.01)/(0.99×0.01+0.01×0.99) ≈ 50%. The base-rate lesson.

modules.title: Tech Math: Trade-Applied Mathematics
modules.summary: Arithmetic fluency through shop mathematics: whole-number operations, fractions/decimals/percents, fact fluency under time, estimation; measurement and units (US customary and metric, dimensional analysis, precision/tolerance, reading instruments); shop math (ratio/proportion, percent applications — markup, waste, discount — area/volume/material estimation, reading drawings and scales); capped by the readiness verification against the aptitude battery.
objectives: Compute fractions, decimals, percents fluently — under time.
Convert units with dimensional analysis; read instruments to their precision.
Estimate materials: area, volume, waste factors from drawings.
Verify readiness against the aptitude battery; diagnose gaps.

notes.title: Arithmetic fluency
notes.body:
**Whole-number operations**, **fractions/decimals/percents** (the conversions: 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5% — instant), **fact fluency under time** (the timed drills), **estimation** (Fermi-style: is it 10 or 100?).

- Fraction fluency: add with unlike denominators, multiply straight across — no calculators on aptitude tests
- Percent: part = percent × whole — markup, discount, waste are all this one formula
- Estimation first, calculation second — catch the order-of-magnitude error before it costs material

notes.title: Measurement and units
notes.body:
**US customary and metric** (both — the trades use both), **dimensional analysis** (units cancel like fractions: ft × 12 in/ft = in), **precision and tolerance** (± 1/16" means something), **reading instruments** (tape, calipers, micrometers — read to the instrument's precision, not beyond).

- Dimensional analysis: write every conversion as a fraction — units guide the arithmetic
- Tolerance: the drawing's ± is the law — measure to decide pass/fail, not curiosity
- Metric-imperial: 25.4 mm = 1 in exactly — the bridge constant

notes.title: Shop mathematics and the capstone
notes.body:
**Ratio and proportion** in the shop (mix ratios, gear ratios, scale), **percent applications** (markup, waste factors, discounts), **area/volume/material estimation** (waste factor × net = order quantity), **reading drawings and scales** (1/4" = 1' — the scale ruler).

**Capstone**: readiness verification against the aptitude battery — timed, comprehensive, with **gap diagnosis** (the report tells you exactly which node to revisit).

- Waste factors: order = net × (1 + waste%) — 10% for simple, 15%+ for complex cuts
- Scale reading: measure the drawing, multiply by the scale — verify with a known dimension
- The capstone is diagnostic, not judgmental — gaps are a study list, not a verdict

cards.back: 0.375 = 37.5%. Instant conversion is the fluency bar.
Units cancel like fractions — write conversions as fractions, let units guide.
1 inch exactly. The bridge constant.
Order = net × (1 + waste%). 10% simple, 15%+ complex.
Measure inches on paper × 4 = feet real. Verify against a known dimension.
Pass/fail band — measure to decide, not from curiosity.

quiz.q: Convert 6 ft to inches via dimensional analysis?
A 3:1 mix needs 12 gallons total. Part A?

modules.title: Electrician Apprenticeship: etA Entrance
modules.summary: The electrical training ALLIANCE path: interim credentials (Constructing Your Future, Electrical Job Information, Applied Codeology, Electrical Theory DC, Construction Drawings), SQ3R technical reading, workplace conduct and well-being, core budgeting and credit, NECA-NEMRA code literacy (finding articles under time), and the algebra readiness fringe for the aptitude batteries.
objectives: Complete the interim credential sequence in order.
Read technically with SQ3R: survey → question → read → recite → review.
Navigate code articles: organization, 'shall' language, exceptions.
Pass the algebra fringe: fractions through functions, number series.

notes.title: Interim credentials and SQ3R
notes.body:
**Interim credentials** in order: Constructing Your Future → Electrical Job Information 1 → Applied Codeology 2023 → Electrical Theory 1 (DC) → Construction Drawings. Each unlocks the next — sequence matters.

**SQ3R technical reading**: **Survey** (headings, figures), **Question** (what must I learn?), **Read** (actively), **Recite** (say it back), **Review** (spaced). Technical reading is reading to *perform* — the test is doing, not recalling.

- DC theory: Ohm's law, series/parallel, power (P=VI) — the physics under everything
- Construction drawings: symbols, schedules, one-lines — read to build
- Recite from memory — recognition is not recall

notes.title: Conduct, budgeting, well-being
notes.body:
**Workplace conduct**: standards, **reporting channels**, **bystander responsibility** — the trade's social contract.

**Core budgeting and credit**: **budget construction** (income − obligations = reality), **credit scores** (payment history, utilization — what moves them), **apprentice-wage planning** (the wage grows; the budget must too).

**Well-Being 101**: physical demands, sleep/nutrition/recovery, stress and help resources — the career is long; the body is the tool.

- Utilization under 30% — the fastest credit lever
- Apprentice wages step up — budget to the step you're on, plan for the next

notes.title: Code literacy and the algebra fringe
notes.body:
**Code literacy**: how articles are organized, **'shall' vs 'shall be permitted'** (mandatory vs permissive — the language of law), **exceptions are never assumed** (read them; they don't transfer), **finding an article under time** (index → chapter → article — the timed drill).

**Algebra readiness fringe**: the aptitude-test algebra — fractions through functions, **number series** (find the pattern: arithmetic, geometric, alternating).

- 'Shall' = must. 'Shall be permitted' = may. Misreading this fails inspections
- Number series: differences first, ratios second, alternation third — the pattern hunt
- Timed article-finding: the index is the map — practice the lookup, not just the reading

cards.back: Survey, Question, Read, Recite, Review — reading to perform.
VI. And V = IR. The DC trinity.
Shall = mandatory. Shall be permitted = allowed. The language of law.
Never assumed — read the specific exception; it doesn't transfer.
Under 30% — the fastest lever on the score.
42 — differences 4,6,8,10,12, so next is 30+12=42 (pattern n(n+1)).

quiz.q: 'Shall be permitted' in a code article means the action is?

modules.title: Quantitative Finance Mathematics
modules.summary: The mathematical prerequisites beneath the quant ladder: measure-theoretic probability (survey) — sigma-algebras, measures, random variables as measurable functions, expectation via integration, convergence modes; stochastic processes — Markov chains, queues and simulation, random walks, Brownian motion; financial mathematics prerequisites — time value of money, returns/variance/covariance, Black-Scholes prerequisites, discrete-time pricing models.
objectives: State the measure-theoretic foundations: sigma-algebras, expectation as integration.
Analyze Markov chains: stationary distributions, absorption.
Price time: present value, returns, variance/covariance, discrete models.
Connect the math to Black-Scholes prerequisites without hand-waving.

notes.title: Measure-theoretic probability (survey)
notes.body:
**Sigma-algebras**: the collections of events we can assign probability to — closure under complement and countable union. **Measures**: probability as a measure (nonnegative, countably additive, total 1).

**Random variables as measurable functions** (X: Ω → ℝ), **expectation via integration** (E[X] = ∫X dP — the grown-up definition), **convergence modes** (a.s., in probability, in distribution, in Lᵖ — the hierarchy).

- The survey level: know the definitions and why they exist — rigor is the point, not computation
- Convergence hierarchy: a.s. ⇒ in prob ⇒ in dist — know the implications
- This is the language the quant literature speaks — fluency, not just familiarity

notes.title: Stochastic processes
notes.body:
**Markov chains**: memoryless transitions, **stationary distributions** (πP = π), absorption, classification of states.

**Queues and simulation**: M/M/1 basics, Little's law (L = λW), Monte Carlo simulation.

**Random walks** and the **Brownian motion preview**: scaling limits, the continuous-time intuition.

- Stationary: solve πP = π with Σπ = 1 — the long-run behavior
- Little's law: average number = arrival rate × average time — deceptively deep
- Simulation: when analysis fails, Monte Carlo answers — with confidence intervals

notes.title: Financial mathematics prerequisites
notes.body:
**Time value of money**: present/future value, discounting — a dollar today ≠ a dollar tomorrow.

**Returns, variance, covariance**: the statistics of portfolios — diversification as variance reduction.

**Black-Scholes prerequisites**: lognormal prices, risk-neutral intuition, the PDE's ingredients (no hand-waving: know what each assumption buys).

**Discrete-time pricing models**: binomial trees — the computable foundation beneath the continuous models.

- Discounting: PV = FV/(1+r)ᵗ — the atom of finance math
- Binomial trees: up/down with risk-neutral probabilities — price by replication
- The prerequisites are the product — Black-Scholes is assembly of these parts

cards.back: Events we can measure: closed under complement and countable unions.
∫X dP — expectation as Lebesgue integral.
πP = π, Σπ = 1 — the chain's long-run behavior.
L = λW — average number = arrival rate × average time.
100/1.05² ≈ $90.70. Discounting.
Replication — risk-neutral probabilities, backward induction.

quiz.explain: a.s. ⇒ in prob ⇒ in dist — the hierarchy.
Solve πP=π: π₀=0.7π₀+0.4π₁, π₀+π₁=1 → π₀=4/7, π₁=3/7.
Covariance < 1 → combined variance < weighted average — the free lunch (almost).

choices: price as if investors risk-neutral — replication determines price
quiz.explain: No-arbitrage + replication — preferences drop out of the price.

scriptLabs.title: Taylor Approximation Laboratory
scriptLabs.brief: Approximate sin(x) with Taylor polynomials of degree 1, 3, 5, 7 at x=0.5; compute actual errors and the Lagrange bound. See convergence happen.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    # TODO: sum_{k=0..n} (-1)^k x^(2k+1) / (2k+1)!
    pass

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={abs(approx-math.sin(x)):.2e}')
scriptLabs.hint: term k: (-1)**k * x**(2*k+1) / math.factorial(2*k+1). n=0 → degree 1, n=3 → degree 7.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math

def taylor_sin(x, n):
    return sum((-1)**k * x**(2*k+1) / math.factorial(2*k+1) for k in range(n+1))

x = 0.5
for n in (0, 1, 2, 3):
    approx = taylor_sin(x, n)
    err = abs(approx - math.sin(x))
    # Lagrange bound: |R| <= |x|^(2n+3)/(2n+3)!
    bound = abs(x)**(2*n+3) / math.factorial(2*n+3)
    print(f'degree {2*n+1}: approx={approx:.10f} error={err:.2e} bound={bound:.2e}')
# Lesson: error collapses as degree grows — approximation with guarantees.

scriptLabs.title: Monte Carlo: π and Confidence
scriptLabs.brief: Estimate π by dart-throwing; show the estimate converging as N grows; compute a 95% confidence interval. Simulation as a numerical method.
scriptLabs.starter:
import math, random

def estimate_pi(n):
    # TODO: n darts in [0,1]^2, count inside quarter circle
    pass

for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    est = estimate_pi(n)
    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} error={abs(est-math.pi):.2e}')
scriptLabs.hint: inside if x*x+y*y<=1. pi ≈ 4*inside/n. SE ≈ sqrt(p(1-p)/n)*4; 95% CI ≈ est ± 1.96*SE.
scriptLabs.solution:
import math, random

def estimate_pi(n):
    inside = sum(1 for _ in range(n)
                 if (lambda x, y: x*x + y*y <= 1)(random.random(), random.random()))
    return 4*inside/n

for n in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    est = estimate_pi(n)
    p = est/4
    se = 4*math.sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
    print(f'N={n}: pi~{est:.5f} err={abs(est-math.pi):.2e} 95%CI=({est-1.96*se:.4f},{est+1.96*se:.4f})')
# Lesson: error shrinks as 1/sqrt(N) — the Monte Carlo rate; CIs quantify it.

scriptLabs.title: Least Squares from Scratch
scriptLabs.brief: Fit y = ax + b to noisy data via the normal equations — no libraries. Then verify against the closed form. The geometry of regression, by hand.
scriptLabs.starter:
# data: noisy line
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
# TODO: solve [sum x^2, sum x; sum x, n] [a; b] = [sum x*y; sum y]  (normal equations)
# print a, b
scriptLabs.solution:
xs = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
ys = [2.1, 3.9, 6.2, 7.8, 10.1]
n = len(xs)
sx, sy = sum(xs), sum(ys)
sxx, sxy = sum(x*x for x in xs), sum(x*y for x, y in zip(xs, ys))
# normal equations: a = (n*Sxy - Sx*Sy)/(n*Sxx - Sx^2)
den = n*sxx - sx*sx
a = (n*sxy - sx*sy)/den
b = (sy - a*sx)/n
print(f'y = {a:.4f}x + {b:.4f}')  # ~ y = 2x + 0.1
# Lesson: least squares is projection — the normal equations are geometry, not magic.

scenarios.title: The A/B Test
scenarios.context: Variant B converts 5.2% vs A's 5.0% over 10k users each. Ship it?

options.text: Statistical significance: z-test for proportions — is 0.2pp real or noise?
options.why: 0.2pp on 10k users needs a significance test — the standard error decides, not the point estimate.
Point estimates without uncertainty are how noise ships to production.

options.text: Not significant — don't ship on this evidence; run longer or accept the null
options.why: p > 0.05: the difference is consistent with noise. Ship on evidence, not hope.
'Trending' without significance is storytelling. The test said: inconclusive.

print(f, abs(f-0.5) < 0.01)

answerBank.q: Where do I start if math is rusty?
answerBank.a: The placement diagnostic — usually Module 2 (tech math) for fluency, then the spine from college algebra. Don't start calculus with shaky algebra; the gate exists to save you months.

answerBank.q: How much math for machine learning?
answerBank.a: Linear algebra (vectors, eigenvalues, SVD), probability (Bayes, distributions, MLE), calculus (gradients, chain rule). That's Module 1's back half — the platform gates IL-07/IL-16 on these nodes.
They're a writing skill: do every exercise, read proofs actively (cover the next line, predict it), and keep a proof journal. Induction first — it's the most mechanical, and it builds the muscle.

answerBank.q: Is the electrician track only for electricians?
answerBank.a: The math (DC theory, shop math) and reading (SQ3R, code literacy) transfer to any trade. The etA credential sequence is electrician-specific; the study skills are universal.

answerBank.q: Quant math without a finance background?
answerBank.a: Yes — the module is prerequisites, not trading. Measure theory, stochastic processes, and time value of money are the language; the ladder (in IL-10's quant track) comes after.
By hand until fluent, then calculator for speed. Exams and job sites test the fluency; the tool is for after you understand.
